title: Who is the patient? A pediatric index-patient filter
line: keeping the medical questions whose primary clinical subject is a child, and dropping the ones that only mention one
question: A keyword sweep for child, infant and adolescent returns far more pediatric questions than are really pediatric. Can the primary clinical subject be identified instead of the vocabulary?
data: 224,705 rows from 16 medical-QA source and configuration subsets
a 269-item calibration set with a held-out split
a 500-row ambiguity audit across 12 failure-mode strata
PedMedQA as an independent, method-different cross-reference

figures.note: the two-stage cascade. a deterministic high-recall keyword and source-scope screen cuts 212,983 rows to 22,834, then a structured classifier that names the primary clinical subject takes that to 12,324. the orange step is the one that would have been the whole method if keywords were enough.

recall is not uniform by age band. the adult-pregnancy gate drops newborns delivered to an adult mother, so neonate recall sits at 75.4%. a validated fix exists and is shipped opt-in rather than on by default, with the gap documented and covered by a test.

links.label: Where it is used: the Growth-MedQA benchmark

calls: the rule is one sentence and it is the whole method: do not classify a question as pediatric just because it contains child terms. identify the primary clinical subject and the target of the question.
the shipped filter is deterministic, dependency-light and needs no API keys. the expensive classifier earned its place by handling the cases the deterministic pass cannot, not by replacing it.

the classifier was improved by rewriting the instructions around primary subject and question target. adding few-shot examples was the wrong lever: the failure mode was keyword surface matching, not a shortage of examples.
every row goes through the same measurement process in one frozen labeling run, rather than routing only prefilter-positive rows to the stronger classifier.
broke: agreement with PedMedQA was nearly reported as validated accuracy before I checked its own labels and found errors in them, including a 19-year-old labeled as an infant. it is a cross-reference and a lower bound, and the docs now say so.
the neonate gap was found by reading recall by age band rather than in aggregate. the aggregate number looked fine.
tried: a sandbox version turned the neonatal override on by default and lifted overall recall to 95.6%. it is not the default because it trades specificity back, so it ships as a flag with the numbers for both settings.
not_shown: the 269-item calibration labels are accepted model labels with a blinded audit, not independent clinician gold. that distinction is in the repo and it matters.
